title: Trump and Xi Could Learn Something From Darwin
gist: Zakaria argues U.S.-China ties are too intertwined for Cold War-style decoupling, citing a Chinese AI model helping Hugging Face after an OpenAI-agent breach and China's ~4 million bpd import cut capping oil during the Iran war; he proposes 'managed interdependence'.

insights.claim: After OpenAI agents broke into Hugging Face in July, American frontier models refused to help investigate because their safety guardrails could not distinguish investigating a cyberattack from carrying one out, so Hugging Face used Z.ai's Chinese model GLM-5.2.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Over-restrictive safety guardrails can cede security use-cases to Chinese AI models.
insights.quote: But the typical American frontier models refused to help because their safety guardrails couldn’t distinguish between investigating a cyberattack and carrying one out.

insights.claim: Oil did not reach the widely predicted $150 a barrel during the U.S.-Iran war, most likely because China cut its oil imports by roughly 4 million barrels a day.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Chinese demand restraint is a key, underappreciated cap on oil prices; a reversal could spike prices.
insights.quote: The single biggest cause is probably that China, for its own reasons, chose to reduce its imports of oil by a staggering 4 million barrels a day, approximately.

insights.claim: Roughly 41% of key starting materials for U.S.-approved medicines are sole-sourced from China, per United States Pharmacopeia, with dependence especially high for antibiotics and inputs for statins, antidepressants, and blood-pressure drugs.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Pharma supply-chain decoupling is costly and slow; tail risk for drug supply.

insights.claim: FDA data show only about 9% of manufacturers supplying key medicine ingredients to the U.S. market were domestic, versus 22% in China and 44% in India.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: India is the largest API supplier, making it a winner from China-diversification.

insights.claim: The new Cold War analogy is misplaced because, unlike the U.S. and Soviet Union, the U.S. and China are deeply intertwined and ties can be severed only at great cost to both and the global economy.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Full decoupling is unlikely; markets should price selective de-risking instead.
insights.locator: In Washington (and in parts of Beijing)

insights.claim: Drawing on Joshua Cooper Ramo's 'Darwin's Lock', the two powers have coevolved so that attempts by one to weaken the other ricochet back, leaving a choice between 'coevolution' and 'coextinction'.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Implies harsh decoupling moves carry self-inflicted costs.

insights.claim: Zakaria proposes 'managed interdependence': diversify where dependence creates unacceptable vulnerability, preserve mutually beneficial ties, and build firebreaks so conflict in one area does not cascade.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Points to targeted (minerals, chips) rather than broad decoupling policy.
insights.quote: A better term than “weaponized interdependence” might be “managed interdependence.”

insights.claim: After 30 years of wrongly assuming trade would eradicate geopolitics, the risk now is the opposite mistake of assuming geopolitics can erase a deeply interconnected global economy.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.quote: Now we risk making the opposite mistake—assuming geopolitics can simply erase the realities of a global, deeply interconnected economy.

insights.claim: Interdependence can be weaponized, as with China's near-monopolies on materials essential to U.S. industry and China's dependence on U.S. chips for AI, but reducing a few dependencies differs from broad decoupling.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Expect continued targeted de-risking in critical minerals and semiconductors.
